references.text: Psalm 105:28 refers directly to the plague of darkness in Egypt: 'He sent darkness and made it dark' (שָׁלַח חֹשֶׁךְ וַיַּחְשִׁךְ). This is a poetic retelling of the ninth plague.
The preceding verse where the Lord commands Moses to stretch out his hand toward heaven to bring darkness over Egypt.
The following verse describing the consequences of the darkness: no one could see each other or leave their place for three days.
Isaiah uses similar imagery of darkness and distress (חֹשֶׁךְ) as God's judgment upon the land.
Joel describes the day of the Lord as 'a day of darkness and gloom' (חֹשֶׁךְ וַאֲפֵלָה), using the same phrase as in Exodus 10:22.
Amos prophesies that the day of the Lord shall be darkness and not light (חֹשֶׁךְ וְלֹא־אוֹר), an eschatological parallel to the plague in Egypt.
Zephaniah describes the day of the Lord with the words 'darkness and gloom' (חֹשֶׁךְ וַאֲפֵלָה), the same expression as the darkness over Egypt.
In Revelation 16:10, the kingdom of the beast is darkened (ἐσκοτωμένη), an eschatological parallel to the darkness of Egypt as God's judgment.
Luke describes a darkness where neither sun nor stars were visible for many days during Paul's sea voyage, echoing the total darkness in Egypt.
The darkness that fell over the whole land (σκότος ἐγένετο ἐπὶ πᾶσαν τὴν γῆν) for three hours at Jesus' crucifixion recalls the darkness in Egypt which lasted three days.
Shows the recurring pattern in the plagues where Moses' hand gesture toward heaven triggers God's judgment.
Concrete parallels between two plagues where Moses' gesture toward heaven unleashes God's power.
Thematic parallel in the structure of the plagues: Moses' action triggers a natural disaster over Egypt.
Typological parallel: The darkness as judgment on Egypt foreshadows the darkness at Jesus' cross as judgment on sin.
